nodes.content: Design a plugin execution service preventing explicit-channel secret exfiltration while supporting authorized streaming releases and concurrent policy revocation.
requirements: Zero unauthorized bytes across 10,000 adversarial executions covering secret transformations and revocation races.
Preserve authorized streaming outputs with under 15% throughput loss versus identical execution without enforcement.

nodes.content: Isolate plugin egress; permit secret-derived streams only through audited declassifiers whose output gate serializes emission with policy revocation.
How can the output gate prevent post-revocation bytes without exceeding 15% throughput overhead during authorized streaming?
A writer-preferring lock spanning each 16-KiB output write should admit zero bytes after revocation commits while adding under 15% overhead.
Stress writer-preferring 16-KiB output gates across 10,000 transformed-secret revocation races; measure post-commit bytes and throughput against ungated streaming.
Across 10,000 revocation races, post-commit bytes were zero, but authorized streaming throughput fell 19% versus ungated execution.
Using 64-KiB writer-preferring gated writes should retain zero post-commit bytes while reducing throughput loss below 15%.
Rerun 10,000 transformed-secret revocation races with 64-KiB gated writes; compare post-commit bytes and authorized-stream throughput against ungated execution.
Across 10,000 races, 64-KiB gating emitted zero unauthorized bytes after revocation commit; authorized-stream throughput fell 11% versus ungated execution.
Adopt 64-KiB writer-preferring gated writes for audited declassifiers: 10,000 races showed zero post-commit bytes and 11% throughput loss.
Implement isolated egress and audited declassifiers with the adopted 64-KiB gate; validate leakage and throughput across 10,000 transformation-and-revocation executions.
Implement EgressBroker v1: sandbox network/filesystem writes, deny raw stdout/stderr, and serialize audited declassifier writes with 64-KiB policy gates.
EgressBroker v1 blocks direct network, filesystem, stdout, and stderr writes; audited declassifiers stream through revocation-serialized 64-KiB gates.
Run LeakRace-10k against EgressBroker v1, fuzzing encoded secrets, explicit egress channels, and revocation timing; measure unauthorized bytes and streaming throughput.
LeakRace-10k found zero unauthorized bytes across 10,000 transformation and revocation attacks; authorized streaming lost 12% throughput versus unenforced execution.
Run StreamPermit-1k to compare authorized output byte-for-byte against ungated streams and assert zero post-commit writes under concurrent revocation.
StreamPermit-1k found 7/1,000 never-revoked streams lost final sub-64-KiB chunks; concurrent races still emitted zero post-commit bytes.
Retain EgressBroker’s gated declassification, but block rollout until partial-chunk flushing is fixed; LeakRace-10k passed, while StreamPermit-1k exposed truncation.
Add an explicit end-of-stream flush under the writer-preferring policy gate, releasing partial chunks only while authorization remains valid.
Can end-of-stream flushing preserve final partial chunks without permitting bytes after revocation commits or exceeding 15% throughput loss?
Gating an explicit end-of-stream flush with the existing writer lock should eliminate partial-chunk truncation without post-commit leaks or 15% overhead.
Implement writer-lock-protected final flushing; rerun StreamPermit-1k and LeakRace-10k, measuring byte equality, post-commit leakage, and throughput.
After gated final flushing, StreamPermit-1k matched all 1,000 authorized streams; LeakRace-10k leaked zero unauthorized bytes, with 13% throughput loss.
Integrate gated final flushing into EgressBroker v1; gate canary rollout on LeakRace-10k, StreamPermit-1k byte equality, and under-15% overhead.
Patch EgressBroker v1 to flush sub-64-KiB tails under its writer-preferring policy gate, rejecting flushes after revocation commits.
EgressBroker v1.1 adds lock-serialized end-of-stream flushing for partial chunks, retaining revocation checks before each output write.
Canary EgressBroker v1.1 with StreamPermit-1k and LeakRace-10k; compare byte fidelity, unauthorized output, and throughput against ungated execution.
Canary EgressBroker v1.1 matched 1,000/1,000 authorized streams; LeakRace-10k found zero unauthorized bytes and 13% throughput loss.
Bind declassifiers to destination-scoped release capabilities specifying permitted transformations and byte budgets; validate capabilities within EgressBroker’s gated writes.
How can EgressBroker enforce shared byte budgets across concurrent streams without overspending or truncating authorized releases?
Atomically debit each capability’s shared budget inside the output gate; reject whole writes exceeding it, preserving releases within budget.
Run BudgetRace-10k with 32 concurrent streams sharing 1-MiB capabilities; check atomic debits, overspend bytes, and in-budget stream fidelity.
BudgetRace-10k showed zero overspend, but 286 runs rejected 64-KiB writes despite 1–63 KiB remaining, wasting authorized capacity.
Run BudgetTail-1k across 1–63-KiB residual budgets and concurrent revocations; measure lost authorized bytes and post-commit leakage.
BudgetTail-1k preserved all 1,000 releases whose writes fit remaining budgets, with zero post-commit leakage during concurrent revocation.
Retain atomic gated debits, but split oversized writes at remaining-budget boundaries; in-budget writes already preserve fidelity without post-commit leakage.
Implement destination-scoped capabilities with atomic gated debits and budget-boundary splitting; rerun BudgetRace-10k and LeakRace-10k, targeting under-15% overhead.
Implement EgressBroker v1.2: validate destination and transformation capabilities, then atomically debit and split writes at remaining-budget boundaries under the gate.
EgressBroker v1.2 adds destination- and transformation-scoped release capabilities, atomic gated byte debits, and budget-boundary splitting for partial writes.
Test EgressBroker v1.2 with BudgetRace-10k and LeakRace-10k; measure overspend, unauthorized bytes, authorized-stream fidelity, and throughput.
BudgetRace-10k found zero overspend or lost authorized tail bytes; LeakRace-10k found zero unauthorized bytes and 14% throughput loss.
Confine plugins in broker-only microVMs, closing inherited descriptors and blocking Unix-socket, pipe, and shared-memory egress bypasses.
Can broker-only microVMs eliminate inherited-descriptor and local-IPC bypasses without pushing authorized streaming overhead above 15%?
Prewarmed microVMs exposing only a broker virtio queue should block local-IPC escapes while keeping streaming overhead under 15%.
Run IPCBreak-10k against prewarmed broker-only microVMs, probing inherited descriptors and local IPC; compare streaming throughput with unenforced execution.
IPCBreak-10k found zero local-IPC escapes, but prewarmed microVMs reduced authorized-stream throughput 19% versus unenforced execution.
Batch four 64-KiB chunks per virtio notification, retaining per-chunk gating; this should preserve zero escapes and reduce overhead below 15%.
Rerun IPCBreak-10k with four-chunk virtio batches and per-chunk gates; measure bypass bytes, post-revocation bytes, and authorized-stream overhead.
IPCBreak-10k found zero bypass or post-revocation bytes, but four-chunk batching still incurred 16% authorized-stream throughput loss.
Profile four-chunk virtio batches across StreamSize-1k workloads, attributing throughput loss to notifications, per-chunk gating, and copies.
StreamSize-1k attributed batching’s overhead reduction from 19% to 16% to fewer virtio notifications; per-chunk gating dominated remaining costs.
Hold one writer-preferring gate lock across each four-chunk batch, retaining per-chunk capability debits; expect zero leaks and under-15% overhead.
Run IPCBreak-10k with batch-held gates and atomic per-chunk debits; measure post-commit bytes, budget overspend, and throughput versus unenforced execution.
IPCBreak-10k found zero bypass, post-commit, or overspend bytes, but batch-held gates still cost 15.4% authorized-stream throughput.
Profile batch-held gates across StreamSize-1k, comparing lock acquisition counts and CPU copy time against per-chunk gating.
StreamSize-1k showed batch-held gates cut lock acquisitions 75% and overhead from 16% to 15.4%; payload copying dominated remaining cost.
Run BatchCompare-10k contrasting per-chunk versus batch-held gates under revocation and shared budgets; measure leakage, lock costs, and throughput.
BatchCompare-10k: contention-heavy streams had zero leakage; per-chunk gating lost 14.7% throughput, versus 15.6% for batch-held gating.
Defer microVM rollout: both batch variants exceed 15% overall; retain per-chunk gates for contention-heavy streams and optimize payload copying.
Prototype read-only shared-buffer virtio transfer with per-chunk gates; rerun IPCBreak-10k, targeting zero leakage and under-15% overhead.
Implement sealed 64-KiB guest buffers for virtio transfer, mapping pages read-only before broker validation and per-chunk gated emission.
MicroVM EgressBroker prototype passes sealed, read-only 64-KiB virtio buffers to per-chunk policy gates, avoiding payload copies.
Run IPCBreak-10k against sealed-buffer microVMs, probing buffer mutation, local-IPC bypasses, revocation leakage, and authorized-stream throughput.
IPCBreak-10k found zero buffer-mutation, local-IPC, or post-commit leaks; authorized streams matched baseline with 13.8% throughput loss.
Adopt sealed-buffer microVMs with per-chunk gates: copying and batch-held locks missed throughput targets; IPCBreak-10k achieved zero leaks at 13.8% loss.
